questions.q: What specific problem does the `src/` layout (library code under `src/<package>/`) prevent, compared to a flat layout with the package at the repo root?
options: It prevents Python from accidentally importing the uninstalled local package directly off the filesystem just because you happen to be running from the repo root, which can mask real packaging problems
It prevents the package from ever having bugs
It removes the need for a pyproject.toml file
It makes the code run faster
questions.explain: With a flat layout, Python's current-directory import behavior can make a script 'work' only because it's run from one specific directory, masking issues that would surface once the package is properly installed and run from elsewhere -- the src/ layout forces imports through the installed package instead.

questions.q: What is `pyproject.toml`'s role in a modern Python project?
options: It replaces the need for any version control
It stores the actual test results from the last pytest run
It is only used for Cython projects
It is the standard, tool-agnostic file for project metadata, dependencies, and build configuration, replacing a bare setup.py
questions.explain: pyproject.toml holds project metadata (name, version, dependencies, optional dev dependencies) and build-system configuration in a standard format most Python tooling now reads.

questions.q: What does `pip install -e .` (an editable install) do, and why does it matter for a research repo?
options: It only works for packages with no dependencies
It installs a read-only, uneditable version of the package
It installs the package pointing at the actual source directory, so edits take effect immediately and imports work consistently from any directory -- not just the repo root
It copies the source code to a temporary folder and deletes the original
questions.explain: Editable mode points Python's import machinery directly at the src/ directory, so scripts, notebooks, and tests can all `import quant_research` the same way regardless of which directory they're launched from, and changes to the source are picked up without reinstalling.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend keeping both loosely-versioned dependencies in `pyproject.toml` AND a pinned lockfile (or requirements.txt)?
options: Because lockfiles are required by Python itself to run any script
Because pyproject.toml cannot list any dependencies at all

Because pyproject.toml's loose ranges (e.g. numpy>=1.24) give flexibility, while a lockfile pins the exact versions actually used in a specific run, which is needed to reproduce that exact result later
Because requirements.txt replaces the need for pyproject.toml entirely
questions.explain: Loose version ranges support general usability and future compatibility, while a lockfile captures the exact dependency versions used for a specific research run -- both serve different, complementary purposes for reproducibility.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should happen to a useful function that starts out written in a notebook cell?
options: It should be copy-pasted into every notebook and script that needs it
It should be deleted and rewritten from scratch in Cython
It should stay in the notebook permanently, since notebooks are the correct home for all research code
It should be promoted into the library under src/<package>/, with a real test added in tests/, rather than being left as logic nobody else can import or test
questions.explain: The lesson frames notebooks and scripts as consumers of the library, not places where new reusable logic should permanently live -- proven-useful code belongs in the tested, importable src/ package.
